articleTitle: The specification and measurement of future radar systems
publicationTitle: IEE Workshop on The Future of Radar in the UK and Europe (Ref. No. 1999/186)
abstract: The successful acquisition of future adaptive radars is likely to require significant changes to procurement methodology. In particular, it is likely that the specification and measurement of performance will require the extensive use of modelling and simulation, at least partly replacing conventional trials measurements. This change in approach will also benefit from detailed and early technical involvement by the customer and user to ensure that their operational requirements are met and that performance provided by the radar is fully understood.

articleTitle: Future radar systems for remote sensing
publicationTitle: IEE Workshop on The Future of Radar in the UK and Europe (Ref. No. 1999/186)
abstract: The goal of the presentation is to point out the state of the art of both SAR-techniques and SAR-technology, to show expected developments for key components and features as well as to present new techniques which are in a promising research stage. The frequency range considered is from about 10 MHz up to about 35 GHz The vision of an autonomous, global, integrated reconnaissance and remote sensing system with communication and positioning capability concludes the presentation.

articleTitle: Future electronically steered antennas for airborne radar
publicationTitle: IEE Workshop on The Future of Radar in the UK and Europe (Ref. No. 1999/186)
abstract: The electronically scanned antenna introduces a technological breakthrough in airborne radar. First the beam agility makes search and tracking completely independent, opens the way to new detection strategies and improves dramatically the tactical situation acquisition. It enables also simultaneous modes implementation. By suppressing the mechanical parts, it increases the reliability, makes easier the platform installation and reduces the antenna RCS. An active electronically scanned antenna (AESA) offers even more potentialities with an improved power budget thanks to loss reduction and beam shaping capabilities which enables one to adapt the radiating pattern to the environment. This paper first describes the operational benefits given by these technologies for the different airborne radar applications i.e. fighter radar, airborne early warning (AEW) systems, air to ground surveillance (AGS) and maritime patrol radar. Then it describes the competing ESA solutions. To conclude, the more suitable solutions are proposed according to the main constraints and requirements related to the different applications.

articleTitle: The future of radar-an academic perspective
publicationTitle: IEE Workshop on The Future of Radar in the UK and Europe (Ref. No. 1999/186)
abstract: British universities have a long and distinguished tradition of work in radar, probably the most spectacular example of which was Randall and Boot's invention of the cavity magnetron at the University of Birmingham in 1940. Nowadays universities have an important role, both in research and education, and this situation is mirrored in other European countries. The paper reviews the status of university contributions to radar, both in the UK and elsewhere, and to consider how this may best develop in the future.

publicationTitle: IEE Workshop on The Future of Radar in the UK and Europe (Ref. No. 1999/186)
abstract: Many developing technologies must be considered in the choice of the future radar markets to be addressed. The understanding of the core and adjacent markets with knowledge of the market size and predicted growth allows the development of business strategies and exploitation of inherent technology synergies. An example high level naval and land air defence radar systems market map is shown. Each market sector may be further broken down to consider the product, competitor and technology information required understand the sales opportunities.

articleTitle: Cost drivers in airborne fighter radar programmes
publicationTitle: IEE Workshop on The Future of Radar in the UK and Europe (Ref. No. 1999/186)
abstract: This paper considers the factors that drive up costs in airborne radar programmes. It concentrates on fighter radars that pose the most difficult technical challenges on account of the complexity required and the constraints applied to volume, mass, power and vibration in the fighter environment. It observes that a comprehensive effort spanning concept, procurement, development and support is needed to achieve the lowest cost. Data is drawn from the development of the ECR 90 radar, now ordered in production quantities for the Eurofighter/Typhoon aircraft.
